值得閱讀的理由

  • 從一支十多人的團隊悄悄把後端從 AWS 換到 Vercel 的故事，看見雲端基礎設施競爭如何改變。
  • 理解創辦人 Guillermo Rauch 如何把「讓建置產品更簡單」的願景，延伸到 AI 代理與企業現代化。
  • 掌握新創聚焦切入市場、逐步擴張，以及透過產品體驗累積信任的實用思路。

摘要

從 AWS 轉向 Vercel：讓雲端基礎設施更簡單

作者以一則出人意料的故事開場：2026 年上半年，一支約十二人的新創團隊趁創辦人休假，悄悄把整套後端基礎設施從 AWS 換到 Vercel。這項轉換沒有事先通報，卻讓團隊降低成本、節省時間，也不必聘請全職基礎設施工程師。Vercel 由 Guillermo Rauch 創立，他也是許多開發者熟悉的 Next.js 框架創辦人；不少熱門 AI 產品也採用 Vercel 的平台。

談到如何與 AWS 這類巨頭競爭時，Rauch 沒有先談市場策略，而是回憶自己初次使用雲端的挫折。過去他曾直接操作實體資料中心，雲端問世後，他原以為能快速開始，結果卻花了整整一個月設定基礎設施與工具，才做出基本產品。這段經驗讓他開始反覆思考：每次解決難題後，能不能把學到的東西做成工具，讓下一次更容易？

因此，Vercel 最初想解決的不是 AI，而是雲端使用門檻太高、流程過於繁瑣的問題。團隊曾把目標稱作「自動駕駛式基礎設施」：使用者只要說明方向，其餘交給系統處理。如今，這樣的理念也與代理技術相呼應。

押注下一波技術，讓小團隊擁有更大產能

Rauch 不認為自己是在與過去使用的技術正面交鋒。他把技術演進看成世代交替：舊技術不會一夕消失，卻會逐漸失去注意力與創新動能。大型企業採用 Vercel，未必是要搬遷二十年前的舊應用，更多時候是因為內部開始使用程式碼代理，或需要新的基礎設施來開發產品。對新創而言，與其逆著逐漸退潮的浪潮掙扎，不如站在下一波需求的前方。

這項判斷也形成了 Vercel 的組織願景：讓規模很小的團隊，具備巨大的業務產能。Rauch 初到矽谷時，曾在 Instagram 起步的共享辦公空間工作。他認為 Instagram 的成功，部分來自當時新推出的 Amazon S3：團隊不用自建機房與儲存設備，只要呼叫 API，就能儲存大量照片。沿著這個方向，他想像未來或許會有一家由一個人經營、估值達兆美元的公司；這不是否定團隊的價值，而是因為如今一個人搭配一群代理，已能完成過去需要數百甚至數千人才能完成的工作。

他也提出「涓滴向上」的現象：成熟企業會關注最前沿的小型團隊；當它們看到十幾個人就能達成難以想像的交付效率，便會感受到現代化壓力。大型公司有時也會直接收購新創，讓 Vercel 的技術隨之進入企業。因此，只要先服務好最具前瞻性的團隊，大企業往往會跟進。

無頭架構與 AI 代理的契合

Rauch 多年來推廣無頭架構，也就是將前端呈現層與後端商業邏輯分離。早期他坦言，推廣這套架構也有希望更多人使用 Next.js 的私心；但他確實相信，後端應提供乾淨、安全、可稽核的 API，前端則能依照業務需求自由演化。這種做法曾在電商領域較容易落地，因為多品牌經營本來就需要把呈現層與後端拆開。

隨著智慧代理興起，這套架構的價值更加明顯。代理需要 API、CLI 與 MCP；後端若能整理成純粹的資料與功能介面，前端便能根據使用者意圖，即時生成個人化體驗。對 Rauch 而言，程式碼代理的爆發，像是多年堅持的架構路線終於獲得驗證。

不過，Vercel 初入市場時也曾犯下常見錯誤：把自己定位成「更好的 AWS」或「更好的 Google」。Rauch 回顧，想要面面俱到、服務所有人，往往會讓新創最後一無所成。市場真正願意付費的，是特定領域裡真正出色的產品；當自動化工具大量產出平庸內容時，突破之道更是拿出品質足以壓倒競品的產品。

從明確切入點擴張，而非盲目多角化

為了擺脫過於寬泛的定位，Rauch 選擇收斂資源，先把少數使用情境做到極致，並以直觀的商業價值證明後端技術的效益。面對企業決策者時，他不再從底層架構談起，而是先談客戶體驗與營收回報。電商成為理想入口：在這個領域，時間就是金錢，應用效能提升 200%，轉換率與營收可能很快就反映出差異；有客戶甚至在財務報告中，直接將營收提升歸因於升級更高效能的底層架構。

這種策略讓他聯想到特斯拉曾公開的商業計畫：先把資源投入少數人負擔得起的高端跑車，並確保產品從一開始就做到業界頂尖。不過，聚焦單一入口還不夠，企業也得預先規劃如何以同心圓方式向外擴張，不能只盯著一個市場區隔。選擇起點時，市場本身也必須夠大，這樣沿著原有主軸才有合理的延伸方向。

擴張過程中，企業必須避免盲目多角化，並留意所謂的「品牌許可」：若市場認定一家公司是專業的基礎設施供應商，它突然轉做消費型冰箱，即使產品不錯，也可能模糊品牌定位並影響內部文化。另一方面，許多物聯網設備雖然仰賴 AWS 後端，使用者卻不必直接接觸 AWS，這也說明基礎設施服務有時適合在幕後發揮作用。

信任是長期打磨產品後的成果

談到開發者為何對 Vercel 有高度忠誠與信任，Rauch 顛覆了常見的品牌觀念。他認為外界看到的設計講究，不只是美學追求，更是一次次存入信任銀行。在通用人工智慧時代，深厚的信任將成為企業重要的護城河；但信任是結果，不是可以直接輸入的手段。品牌信任、開發者體驗與產品品質，都是把事情做好後才會顯現的成果。

他表示，Vercel 最有利於品牌的作為，往往不是刻意經營品牌時做出的，而是團隊日復一日打磨客戶體驗、執著於令人愉悅的細節。他以健身作比喻：光是不斷做仰臥起坐，未必就能練出腹肌；真正重要的是飲食、睡眠與整體健康管理。字幕在此處截斷，作者未能完整轉述這段比喻後續的內容。

Hello everyone, this is Best Partner, I'm Da Fei. Let me start with something that sounds a bit outrageous. In the first half of 2026, a startup team of a dozen people was refactoring their system, and the founder happened to be on vacation. When he returned, the entire backend infrastructure had been quietly switched by the team from Amazon AWS to WSO. There was no warning and no prior report, and the reason was quite practical: costs dropped, time was saved , and they no longer needed to hire a full-time infrastructure engineer. This is the opening of this interview, from an episode of the DF podcast released on. October 29th. The company that pulled off the "sneak attack" is WSO, founded by Guillermo Rauch, whose Next.js is used by many developers every day. Quite a few popular AI products in Silicon Valley also run on his platform. Reports mentioned that WSO's valuation reached $ 9.3 billion in 2025. Since I use WSO myself, I was very interested in this episode, so today I'd like to share it with you all. Normally, when asked how to compete with a giant like AWS, a founder would talk about strategy, but Rauch didn't; he first talked about his first experience using the cloud. Before. that, he had spent years writing code in environments where he had to directly operate physical data centers. After cloud computing emerged, he excitedly tried it out, only to end up feeling frustrated; he felt he had to spend an entire month just configuring infrastructure and tools to get a basic product running. As an engineer who had been programming for years, facing the cloud made him feel a bit foolish, a feeling he has always remembered. His habit of building products is actually related to this experience; every time he solves a difficult problem, he asks himself: can what I learned be turned. into a tool to make the next time easier ? So, what WSO originally wanted to solve wasn't AI, but the usability of the cloud. The cloud gave us nearly infinite computing power, and today's wave of super-intelligence is built upon it, but for most people, the barrier is still too high and the process too tedious. Internally, they once called what they were building "self-driving infrastructure," meaning to make building products like driving a self-driving car—you just give the direction, and the system handles the rest. Today, everyone calls this agent. technology. There is a key attitude here : Guillermo says he never feels like he is competing head-on with the solutions he left behind. He wants to build next-generation solutions, so the fear of competition has never even crossed his mind. He views technology as a generational issue. Old technology rarely disappears overnight; it just gradually loses attention and innovative potential. Legacy machines are still in use today, and he himself relies heavily on instant messaging, though he still occasionally sends and receives emails. While old technology will persist for a long time, what he truly cares about is.

what will be needed most in the future. Just like many large enterprises today using Vercel, it’s not because they want to migrate 20-year-old apps, but because they are internally using many coding agents or need new infrastructure to develop their own. For startups, his advice is straightforward: instead of struggling against an old wave losing momentum, it’s better to position yourself right in front of the next one . Applied to organizations, this judgment becomes a concrete ambition: to enable tiny teams to possess massive business throughput capabilities. When he first arrived in Silicon Valley, the. co-working space he worked in happened to be where Instagram started. It was an app intended to challenge the entire social network, yet its core team was shockingly small. A crucial reason Instagram succeeded was that they leveraged the then-newly launched Amazon S3. Without needing to set up their own racks and storage, they could store massive amounts of photos by just calling a few APIs. Following this logic , he suggests that perhaps one day, Vercel will help spawn a trillion-dollar company run by a single person. He says this isn't denying the value of teams; he sees every day how one person plus a group of agents can do the work that. used to require hundreds or even thousands of people. So what about large enterprises? He says there is a " trickle-up effect." Mature companies keep an eye on cutting-edge creative teams, and when they see a dozen people achieving unimaginable delivery efficiency, they get anxious and develop a demand for modernization. Therefore, as long as you serve the most forward-thinking group well, large enterprises will often follow suit on their own. Sometimes large companies will directly acquire startup teams, and in this way, Vercel's technology enters the large company as well. The architectural pressure within enterprises is also erupting; Guillermo has been promoting headless architecture for many years, completely decoupling. the frontend presentation layer from the backend business logic. He admits that early on, he had a selfish motive for promoting this—he wanted Next.js to be used by more people. It’s like building a new appliance; you have to ensure there are compatible outlets worldwide. He truly believed in this architecture: a backend with clean, secure, and auditable APIs, while the frontend evolves into any interaction model the business requires. He spent years preaching this philosophy with great difficulty, but it only really clicked within the e-commerce industry. Due to the multi-brand nature of e-commerce, the presentation layer must be decoupled. from the backend. When the era of intelligent agents arrived, everyone realized this architecture was the perfect soil. Agents crave APIs, CLIs, and MCPs. Once the backend settles into pure data and functional interfaces, the frontend can generate personalized experiences in real-time based on user intent. Leo says this makes him feel like an overnight success; the explosion of code agents has essentially validated the path he has stubbornly followed for years. However, the path taken at the beginning was still quite naive. When first entering the market, they marketed themselves as a better AWS or a better.

Google. Looking back, he sees this as the most common pitfall for startups— trying to be everything to everyone and often ending up with nothing. The commercial market only pays for excellence in specific domains. Faced with a flood of mediocre content generated by automation tools, the most effective way to break through is to deliver a product with absolute, overwhelming quality. So, he executed a strategic retreat, focusing his energy on perfecting a few scenarios and using the most intuitive business value to prove the backend. From then on, when talking to corporate decision-makers, he stopped starting with underlying architecture and began with customer. experience and business returns. E-commerce was the perfect entry point. In this field, time is money. If you improve application performance by 200% , the conversion rate on the books will react overnight. To this day, he still hears this kind of feedback from client management teams every single day. Sometimes clients even write in their financial reports that revenue jumped directly because they upgraded to a higher-performance underlying architecture. This logic is clean and very difficult to refute. This strategy of contraction follows the secret master plan Tesla once published: first, put all your resources into a single, stunning high-end sports car for a. select few, but ensure it is industry-leading from day one, leaving no room for mediocrity. But having a narrow entry point isn't enough; he says a business plan must include a strategy for concentric expansion, radiating outward from a single point of origin. If your strategy map only has one market segment with no subsequent moves, your business will quickly hit a ceiling; you must plan ahead like in a game of chess . To find extensions beyond your starting point, there’s a prerequisite: the market you enter must be large enough. From the very beginning, they locked onto cloud computing infrastructure. So, by following the. main thread, you can always find logical points of extension. During this process , you must be wary of blind diversification. He mentioned a concept called "brand permission." If a company is known today as a professional infrastructure provider and suddenly announces it will build consumer refrigerators tomorrow, even with a great product, the market’s perception becomes blurred and internal culture suffers. He added an interesting point: "Although many IoT devices run on their backend services, most people never interact with AWS directly, so they are happy to remain behind the scenes." At. this point, the host asked something many are curious about: with such strong loyalty and trust among developers, how is that cultivated? His answer turned conventional wisdom on its head. He said that while outsiders see their near-obsession with design as an aesthetic pursuit, he views these refinements as deposits into a bank of trust. In the post-AGI era, deep trust will be one of the most important moats for business organizations, but trust is an output, not an input. He often shares this mental model with entrepreneurs: brand trust, and to an extent, developer.

experience and product quality, are things measured only after you've finished the job, not actions you perform directly. Many ask him, how exactly do you build a brand? He says the most "correct" things they’ve done for the brand were the ones where they weren't thinking about branding at all. They simply spent day after day polishing customer experiences and obsessing over delightful details; he used a fitness analogy: you don't get shredded abs just by doing endless crunches; they are made in the kitchen. What you really need to control is your. diet, sleep, and overall health management; crunches are just for finishing touches. Running a company is exactly the same. Posting more tweets, hosting offline events, or making a website look pretty—these are just " crunches." The real input includes underlying certainty, system security, tracking every bug to the end until it's fixed, clear architecture, and solid documentation. He says that trust in a technology is something built up through accumulated experiences. You might not track it intentionally, but you’ll likely have five to seven scattered encounters—using their product here, clicking a blog post there, or seeing a. comment from their CEO. These scattered signals eventually merge into an intuition that this company's products are reliable; he brought this standard into developer tools, a field that was originally quite rough. One source of this is the sense of order and minimalist aesthetic that Apple absorbed from Braun's industrial design. He wondered, why not bring that same restraint for detail found in consumer electronics into the tools engineers use every day? Back then, open-source projects rarely even had properly formatted READMEs, let alone designed logos or dedicated feature introduction sites. Today, these things have already. become industry standards. He says a deeper reason is that you must respect your own true standards; if you value a certain product quality and enjoy specific service interactions in life, do you hold your team to those same standards every day? This kind of insistence is painful in management; when you look around every day, all you see are unfinished works that aren't perfect enough. You have to maintain a rational dissatisfaction with the status quo, while being able to paint a clear blueprint and lead the team in making incremental improvements. Then, he offered a piece of advice that hits even harder. Sometimes, when he goes to the gym, he sees people who stay for an hour. , spending most of the time on their phones and doing a few sets before calling it quits. You're physically there, but you're not actually training . Once, at a small hotel gym, he noticed someone who stayed as long as he did but trained ten times harder, enduring ten times the pain in the process. He says many companies are the same: they run as usual every day, looking very busy, but they aren't enduring the pain that entrepreneurship should rightfully involve. Specifically, they don't proactively ask core customers what exactly makes the product frustrating, they ignore the survey forms users fill out when they churn, and they lack the.

courage to follow up with each customer who left due to a poor experience. Much of this so-called diligence is just using routine busywork to avoid the mental pain of facing defects head-on. So, how do you catch these problems? He says that with an engineer's mindset, you might as well design the company itself like a system. Beyond external clients, he is equally focused on internal collaboration. They opened a public channel in their internal software called "Developer Experience Complaints," where employees can voice any issues that cause extreme inefficiency or block their work. He has set this channel to the highest notification priority, and he reads. every single message himself. His logic is that the state of internal company collaboration will inevitably be projected onto the products delivered externally; it would be just as strange as Apple employees using Android phones . Now, they have an additional subject of observation: AI agents. How agents use their platform and whether it works smoothly have also been added to their daily optimization checklist. Speaking of users, WS's customer base has changed three times in recent years: first it was technical personnel, then "no-code" allowed non-technical users to build things, and now there is a brand-new class of customers: AI agents. Hou. doesn't see these as three fragmented markets; he views user technical ability as a continuous spectrum. From day one, WS has been doing the same thing: lowering the entry barrier for building digital products while keeping the ceiling sufficiently high. There is a layer of filtering involved; he says they won't cater to users who don't seek excellence or want to keep learning, and AI agents are currently blurring the lines between technical and non-technical staff. He prefers a different term: "builders." He mentioned that many AI tools now default to choosing WS when generating and. deploying code. So, do marketing, customer service, and product design all need to change to cater to AI agents? He first established a prerequisite: he says we cannot hand over the power of thought, choice, and judgment. Even if agents always choose you, you should not abandon your own intent and judgment. He is happy that agents like WS, but he expects his company not to try to manipulate this choice, and hopes model labs don't do it either. He cited a saying from Stripe co-founder Patrick Collison. In an ideal world, AI agents will become the world's most seamless. information and product discovery system . They won't be fooled by exaggerated marketing or swayed by fancy packaging, but will instead lay all options before you, considering both up-and-coming challengers and established products while tailoring to your actual situation . A paradox is emerging here, which he calls the "Autonomy Paradox." The most ideal experience is to leave a requirement and walk away, only to return and find that the product is already live. But while you were away, the agent made thousands of architectural choices and boundary decisions for you. The industry is increasingly favoring agents for long-cycle tasks, and humans are handing.

over more and more control. To reach its goal, an agent might violate safety guardrails or even use non-compliant methods. He’s seen an agent attack another company just because it fit its definition of the task. He takes this issue of agent agency very seriously, even though WS is currently benefiting from it. So, how do we prevent this internally? He says the engineering focus is shifting from frameworks and developer experience to verification and evaluation. Engineers no longer have the model write every line of code; instead , they draw compliance red lines and build closed-loop verification systems. One principle he’s held for years is that verification must be done at the system's outermost edge, as close to the real user as possible, by running full integration tests. He once wrote a famous line: "Write tests, but not too many; focus mainly on integration tests ." Now, everyone is starting to accept this, because they’ve been burned—an agent can quickly write 2 million unit tests and deliver a pile of garbage. You look at the tests and your scalp tingles . It solemnly verifies that 1 + 1 = 2. He’s even seen a test in the internal codebase named something like "This. Constant Equals M-So-and-So." He says this kind of formalism is dangerous; don't be fooled by impressive-looking code metrics. He doesn’t care much about what data structures, algorithms, or libraries you use; he cares whether the product actually works well when the customer gets it. But another point is that understanding itself cannot be compromised. So, the verification loop must be written by humans, because that’s the foundation of confidence when delivering to customers and the key to figuring out why things go wrong. He even extrapolated a bigger judgment: humanity's core work moving forward is capital allocation. Today's hot topic is. safety. Many are busy using AI to build cool things, forgetting that systems still need to be secure, and then they have to pour massive amounts of tokens, budget, and time into 24/7 security audit logs. What managers must do is decide where these resources go, for example, whether to make WS more agent-driven or to thicken the underlying security boundaries. Agents will also constantly push these trade-off problems back onto humans. A few days ago, I had an agent perform extreme optimization on low-level performance, where the program was split into a parser, a scanner, and a checker . When optimization reaches a certain point, the agent stops on its own,. telling us we're already fast enough. Online, this is diminishing returns; it might take another 1,000 hours, do you really want to do that? He says in the future, there will be many such conversations where agents come to you with trade-offs, requests for more budget, and even suggestions. Some have already configured these agents to wake them up in the middle of the night, because difficult trade-offs shouldn't wait until morning. He laughs and says he doesn't recommend doing that, but no matter how powerful the agent is, it works for you, and you are the one who makes the final call. Where capital flows and where the night goes—those decisions must be made by humans. He.

even envisions a more distant form. He visited several teams building fully autonomous companies, where people only act as investors, giving the system startup capital, while a master agent allocates the budget and drives growth, marketing, sales, and engineering. This approach has already proven feasible on a small scale, so should the logic of buying software change? He says you have to re-calculate, especially regarding long-term maintenance costs. There are two types of software that will be strictly phased out within companies. One is the crude tools that existed just to lower the barrier to entry, where four or five specialized programs do the same thing, aiming for accessibility. rather than being the best in their class. Now that the barrier to code generation has been leveled, code can solve math problems, generate images, and create videos; a single coding agent with automated deployment can often replace four or five vendors. The other type is closed systems that refuse to open up to agents. If a piece of software still refuses to provide machine-readable interfaces today, it is blocking an organization’s path to intelligence—it's like a company in the early days of the internet declaring it didn't need to go online. Therefore, the success of MCP makes him particularly happy. His take is that MCP is essentially the HTTP of the agent era. Over 30 years ago, the Hypertext Transfer Protocol brought webpages to our eyes; today, standardized context protocols allow different agents to seamlessly call data and tools. Besides protocols, there is performance; agents will repeatedly call the same interface , so interfaces cannot have heavy rate-limiting, and data must remain consistent. He says the current software world is actually built on many interfaces that lie and crash at any moment. 值得閱讀的理由

  • 從一支十多人的團隊悄悄把後端從 AWS 換到 Vercel 的故事，看見雲端基礎設施競爭如何改變。
  • 理解創辦人 Guillermo Rauch 如何把「讓建置產品更簡單」的願景，延伸到 AI 代理與企業現代化。
  • 掌握新創聚焦切入市場、逐步擴張，以及透過產品體驗累積信任的實用思路。

摘要

從 AWS 轉向 Vercel：讓雲端基礎設施更簡單

作者以一則出人意料的故事開場：2026 年上半年，一支約十二人的新創團隊趁創辦人休假，悄悄把整套後端基礎設施從 AWS 換到 Vercel。這項轉換沒有事先通報，卻讓團隊降低成本、節省時間，也不必聘請全職基礎設施工程師。Vercel 由 Guillermo Rauch 創立，他也是許多開發者熟悉的 Next.js 框架創辦人；不少熱門 AI 產品也採用 Vercel 的平台。

談到如何與 AWS 這類巨頭競爭時，Rauch 沒有先談市場策略，而是回憶自己初次使用雲端的挫折。過去他曾直接操作實體資料中心，雲端問世後，他原以為能快速開始，結果卻花了整整一個月設定基礎設施與工具，才做出基本產品。這段經驗讓他開始反覆思考：每次解決難題後，能不能把學到的東西做成工具，讓下一次更容易？

因此，Vercel 最初想解決的不是 AI，而是雲端使用門檻太高、流程過於繁瑣的問題。團隊曾把目標稱作「自動駕駛式基礎設施」：使用者只要說明方向，其餘交給系統處理。如今，這樣的理念也與代理技術相呼應。

押注下一波技術，讓小團隊擁有更大產能

Rauch 不認為自己是在與過去使用的技術正面交鋒。他把技術演進看成世代交替：舊技術不會一夕消失，卻會逐漸失去注意力與創新動能。大型企業採用 Vercel，未必是要搬遷二十年前的舊應用，更多時候是因為內部開始使用程式碼代理，或需要新的基礎設施來開發產品。對新創而言，與其逆著逐漸退潮的浪潮掙扎，不如站在下一波需求的前方。

這項判斷也形成了 Vercel 的組織願景：讓規模很小的團隊，具備巨大的業務產能。Rauch 初到矽谷時，曾在 Instagram 起步的共享辦公空間工作。他認為 Instagram 的成功，部分來自當時新推出的 Amazon S3：團隊不用自建機房與儲存設備，只要呼叫 API，就能儲存大量照片。沿著這個方向，他想像未來或許會有一家由一個人經營、估值達兆美元的公司；這不是否定團隊的價值，而是因為如今一個人搭配一群代理，已能完成過去需要數百甚至數千人才能完成的工作。

他也提出「涓滴向上」的現象：成熟企業會關注最前沿的小型團隊；當它們看到十幾個人就能達成難以想像的交付效率，便會感受到現代化壓力。大型公司有時也會直接收購新創，讓 Vercel 的技術隨之進入企業。因此，只要先服務好最具前瞻性的團隊，大企業往往會跟進。

無頭架構與 AI 代理的契合

Rauch 多年來推廣無頭架構，也就是將前端呈現層與後端商業邏輯分離。早期他坦言，推廣這套架構也有希望更多人使用 Next.js 的私心；但他確實相信，後端應提供乾淨、安全、可稽核的 API，前端則能依照業務需求自由演化。這種做法曾在電商領域較容易落地，因為多品牌經營本來就需要把呈現層與後端拆開。

隨著智慧代理興起，這套架構的價值更加明顯。代理需要 API、CLI 與 MCP；後端若能整理成純粹的資料與功能介面，前端便能根據使用者意圖，即時生成個人化體驗。對 Rauch 而言，程式碼代理的爆發，像是多年堅持的架構路線終於獲得驗證。

不過，Vercel 初入市場時也曾犯下常見錯誤：把自己定位成「更好的 AWS」或「更好的 Google」。Rauch 回顧，想要面面俱到、服務所有人，往往會讓新創最後一無所成。市場真正願意付費的，是特定領域裡真正出色的產品；當自動化工具大量產出平庸內容時，突破之道更是拿出品質足以壓倒競品的產品。

從明確切入點擴張，而非盲目多角化

為了擺脫過於寬泛的定位，Rauch 選擇收斂資源，先把少數使用情境做到極致，並以直觀的商業價值證明後端技術的效益。面對企業決策者時，他不再從底層架構談起，而是先談客戶體驗與營收回報。電商成為理想入口：在這個領域，時間就是金錢，應用效能提升 200%，轉換率與營收可能很快就反映出差異；有客戶甚至在財務報告中，直接將營收提升歸因於升級更高效能的底層架構。

這種策略讓他聯想到特斯拉曾公開的商業計畫：先把資源投入少數人負擔得起的高端跑車，並確保產品從一開始就做到業界頂尖。不過，聚焦單一入口還不夠，企業也得預先規劃如何以同心圓方式向外擴張，不能只盯著一個市場區隔。選擇起點時，市場本身也必須夠大，這樣沿著原有主軸才有合理的延伸方向。

擴張過程中，企業必須避免盲目多角化，並留意所謂的「品牌許可」：若市場認定一家公司是專業的基礎設施供應商，它突然轉做消費型冰箱，即使產品不錯，也可能模糊品牌定位並影響內部文化。另一方面，許多物聯網設備雖然仰賴 AWS 後端，使用者卻不必直接接觸 AWS，這也說明基礎設施服務有時適合在幕後發揮作用。

信任是長期打磨產品後的成果

談到開發者為何對 Vercel 有高度忠誠與信任，Rauch 顛覆了常見的品牌觀念。他認為外界看到的設計講究，不只是美學追求，更是一次次存入信任銀行。在通用人工智慧時代，深厚的信任將成為企業重要的護城河；但信任是結果，不是可以直接輸入的手段。品牌信任、開發者體驗與產品品質，都是把事情做好後才會顯現的成果。

他表示，Vercel 最有利於品牌的作為，往往不是刻意經營品牌時做出的，而是團隊日復一日打磨客戶體驗、執著於令人愉悅的細節。他以健身作比喻：光是不斷做仰臥起坐，未必就能練出腹肌；真正重要的是飲食、睡眠與整體健康管理。字幕在此處截斷，作者未能完整轉述這段比喻後續的內容。

Hello everyone, this is Best Partner, I'm Da Fei. Let me start with something that sounds a bit outrageous. His habit of building products is actually related to this experience; every time he solves a difficult problem, he asks himself: can what I learned be turned. into a tool to make the next time easier ? Internally, they once called what they were building "self-driving infrastructure," meaning to make building products like driving a self-driving car—you just give the direction, and the system handles the rest. Today, everyone calls this agent. technology. There is a key attitude here : Guillermo says he never feels like he is competing head-on with the solutions he left behind. He wants to build next-generation solutions, so the fear of competition has never even crossed his mind. He views technology as a generational issue. what will be needed most in the future. Following this logic , he suggests that perhaps one day, Vercel will help spawn a trillion-dollar company run by a single person. Mature companies keep an eye on cutting-edge creative teams, and when they see a dozen people achieving unimaginable delivery efficiency, they get anxious and develop a demand for modernization. The architectural pressure within enterprises is also erupting; Guillermo has been promoting headless architecture for many years, completely decoupling. the frontend presentation layer from the backend business logic. He admits that early on, he had a selfish motive for promoting this—he wanted Next.js to be used by more people. It’s like building a new appliance; you have to ensure there are compatible outlets worldwide. He truly believed in this architecture: a backend with clean, secure, and auditable APIs, while the frontend evolves into any interaction model the business requires. He spent years preaching this philosophy with great difficulty, but it only really clicked within the e-commerce industry. Due to the multi-brand nature of e-commerce, the presentation layer must be decoupled. from the backend. When the era of intelligent agents arrived, everyone realized this architecture was the perfect soil. Agents crave APIs, CLIs, and MCPs. Once the backend settles into pure data and functional interfaces, the frontend can generate personalized experiences in real-time based on user intent. Leo says this makes him feel like an overnight success; the explosion of code agents has essentially validated the path he has stubbornly followed for years. However, the path taken at the beginning was still quite naive. When first entering the market, they marketed themselves as a better AWS or a better.

Google. Looking back, he sees this as the most common pitfall for startups— trying to be everything to everyone and often ending up with nothing. experience and product quality, are things measured only after you've finished the job, not actions you perform directly. Many ask him, how exactly do you build a brand? The real input includes underlying certainty, system security, tracking every bug to the end until it's fixed, clear architecture, and solid documentation. You might not track it intentionally, but you’ll likely have five to seven scattered encounters—using their product here, clicking a blog post there, or seeing a. comment from their CEO. These scattered signals eventually merge into an intuition that this company's products are reliable; he brought this standard into developer tools, a field that was originally quite rough. Once, at a small hotel gym, he noticed someone who stayed as long as he did but trained ten times harder, enduring ten times the pain in the process. He says many companies are the same: they run as usual every day, looking very busy, but they aren't enduring the pain that entrepreneurship should rightfully involve. courage to follow up with each customer who left due to a poor experience. Much of this so-called diligence is just using routine busywork to avoid the mental pain of facing defects head-on. So, how do you catch these problems? He says that with an engineer's mindset, you might as well design the company itself like a system. Beyond external clients, he is equally focused on internal collaboration. They opened a public channel in their internal software called "Developer Experience Complaints," where employees can voice any issues that cause extreme inefficiency or block their work. He has set this channel to the highest notification priority, and he reads. every single message himself. His logic is that the state of internal company collaboration will inevitably be projected onto the products delivered externally; it would be just as strange as Apple employees using Android phones . Now, they have an additional subject of observation: AI agents. How agents use their platform and whether it works smoothly have also been added to their daily optimization checklist. Speaking of users, WS's customer base has changed three times in recent years: first it was technical personnel, then "no-code" allowed non-technical users to build things, and now there is a brand-new class of customers: AI agents. Hou. doesn't see these as three fragmented markets; he views user technical ability as a continuous spectrum. From day one, WS has been doing the same thing: lowering the entry barrier for building digital products while keeping the ceiling sufficiently high. There is a layer of filtering involved; he says they won't cater to users who don't seek excellence or want to keep learning, and AI agents are currently blurring the lines between technical and non-technical staff. He prefers a different term: "builders." He mentioned that many AI tools now default to choosing WS when generating and. deploying code. So, do marketing, customer service, and product design all need to change to cater to AI agents? He first established a prerequisite: he says we cannot hand over the power of thought, choice, and judgment. Even if agents always choose you, you should not abandon your own intent and judgment. He is happy that agents like WS, but he expects his company not to try to manipulate this choice, and hopes model labs don't do it either. He cited a saying from Stripe co-founder Patrick Collison. In an ideal world, AI agents will become the world's most seamless. information and product discovery system . A paradox is emerging here, which he calls the "Autonomy Paradox." The most ideal experience is to leave a requirement and walk away, only to return and find that the product is already live. over more and more control. To reach its goal, an agent might violate safety guardrails or even use non-compliant methods. He says this kind of formalism is dangerous; don't be fooled by impressive-looking code metrics. He doesn’t care much about what data structures, algorithms, or libraries you use; he cares whether the product actually works well when the customer gets it. But another point is that understanding itself cannot be compromised. So, the verification loop must be written by humans, because that’s the foundation of confidence when delivering to customers and the key to figuring out why things go wrong. He even extrapolated a bigger judgment: humanity's core work moving forward is capital allocation. Today's hot topic is. safety. Many are busy using AI to build cool things, forgetting that systems still need to be secure, and then they have to pour massive amounts of tokens, budget, and time into 24/7 security audit logs. What managers must do is decide where these resources go, for example, whether to make WS more agent-driven or to thicken the underlying security boundaries. Agents will also constantly push these trade-off problems back onto humans. A few days ago, I had an agent perform extreme optimization on low-level performance, where the program was split into a parser, a scanner, and a checker . When optimization reaches a certain point, the agent stops on its own,. telling us we're already fast enough. Online, this is diminishing returns; it might take another 1,000 hours, do you really want to do that? He says in the future, there will be many such conversations where agents come to you with trade-offs, requests for more budget, and even suggestions. Some have already configured these agents to wake them up in the middle of the night, because difficult trade-offs shouldn't wait until morning. He laughs and says he doesn't recommend doing that, but no matter how powerful the agent is, it works for you, and you are the one who makes the final call. even envisions a more distant form. Now that the barrier to code generation has been leveled, code can solve math problems, generate images, and create videos; a single coding agent with automated deployment can often replace four or five vendors. The other type is closed systems that refuse to open up to agents. If a piece of software still refuses to provide machine-readable interfaces today, it is blocking an organization’s path to intelligence—it's like a company in the early days of the internet declaring it didn't need to go online. Therefore, the success of MCP makes him particularly happy. His take is that MCP is essentially the HTTP of the agent era. Over 30 years ago, the Hypertext Transfer Protocol brought webpages to our eyes; today, standardized context protocols allow different agents to seamlessly call data and tools. sub-agents." The host asked him, as an engineer who reached this point through hardcore programming, how he teaches his children to think deeply in a world almost entirely covered by AI? 值得閱讀的理由

  • 從一支十多人的團隊悄悄把後端從 AWS 換到 Vercel 的故事，看見雲端基礎設施競爭如何改變。
  • 理解創辦人 Guillermo Rauch 如何把「讓建置產品更簡單」的願景，延伸到 AI 代理與企業現代化。
  • 掌握新創聚焦切入市場、逐步擴張，以及透過產品體驗累積信任的實用思路。

摘要

從 AWS 轉向 Vercel：讓雲端基礎設施更簡單

作者以一則出人意料的故事開場：2026 年上半年，一支約十二人的新創團隊趁創辦人休假，悄悄把整套後端基礎設施從 AWS 換到 Vercel。這項轉換沒有事先通報，卻讓團隊降低成本、節省時間，也不必聘請全職基礎設施工程師。Vercel 由 Guillermo Rauch 創立，他也是許多開發者熟悉的 Next.js 框架創辦人；不少熱門 AI 產品也採用 Vercel 的平台。

談到如何與 AWS 這類巨頭競爭時，Rauch 沒有先談市場策略，而是回憶自己初次使用雲端的挫折。過去他曾直接操作實體資料中心，雲端問世後，他原以為能快速開始，結果卻花了整整一個月設定基礎設施與工具，才做出基本產品。這段經驗讓他開始反覆思考：每次解決難題後，能不能把學到的東西做成工具，讓下一次更容易？

因此，Vercel 最初想解決的不是 AI，而是雲端使用門檻太高、流程過於繁瑣的問題。團隊曾把目標稱作「自動駕駛式基礎設施」：使用者只要說明方向，其餘交給系統處理。如今，這樣的理念也與代理技術相呼應。

押注下一波技術，讓小團隊擁有更大產能

Rauch 不認為自己是在與過去使用的技術正面交鋒。他把技術演進看成世代交替：舊技術不會一夕消失，卻會逐漸失去注意力與創新動能。大型企業採用 Vercel，未必是要搬遷二十年前的舊應用，更多時候是因為內部開始使用程式碼代理，或需要新的基礎設施來開發產品。對新創而言，與其逆著逐漸退潮的浪潮掙扎，不如站在下一波需求的前方。

這項判斷也形成了 Vercel 的組織願景：讓規模很小的團隊，具備巨大的業務產能。Rauch 初到矽谷時，曾在 Instagram 起步的共享辦公空間工作。他認為 Instagram 的成功，部分來自當時新推出的 Amazon S3：團隊不用自建機房與儲存設備，只要呼叫 API，就能儲存大量照片。沿著這個方向，他想像未來或許會有一家由一個人經營、估值達兆美元的公司；這不是否定團隊的價值，而是因為如今一個人搭配一群代理，已能完成過去需要數百甚至數千人才能完成的工作。

他也提出「涓滴向上」的現象：成熟企業會關注最前沿的小型團隊；當它們看到十幾個人就能達成難以想像的交付效率，便會感受到現代化壓力。大型公司有時也會直接收購新創，讓 Vercel 的技術隨之進入企業。因此，只要先服務好最具前瞻性的團隊，大企業往往會跟進。

無頭架構與 AI 代理的契合

Rauch 多年來推廣無頭架構，也就是將前端呈現層與後端商業邏輯分離。早期他坦言，推廣這套架構也有希望更多人使用 Next.js 的私心；但他確實相信，後端應提供乾淨、安全、可稽核的 API，前端則能依照業務需求自由演化。這種做法曾在電商領域較容易落地，因為多品牌經營本來就需要把呈現層與後端拆開。

隨著智慧代理興起，這套架構的價值更加明顯。代理需要 API、CLI 與 MCP；後端若能整理成純粹的資料與功能介面，前端便能根據使用者意圖，即時生成個人化體驗。對 Rauch 而言，程式碼代理的爆發，像是多年堅持的架構路線終於獲得驗證。

不過，Vercel 初入市場時也曾犯下常見錯誤：把自己定位成「更好的 AWS」或「更好的 Google」。Rauch 回顧，想要面面俱到、服務所有人，往往會讓新創最後一無所成。市場真正願意付費的，是特定領域裡真正出色的產品；當自動化工具大量產出平庸內容時，突破之道更是拿出品質足以壓倒競品的產品。

從明確切入點擴張，而非盲目多角化

為了擺脫過於寬泛的定位，Rauch 選擇收斂資源，先把少數使用情境做到極致，並以直觀的商業價值證明後端技術的效益。面對企業決策者時，他不再從底層架構談起，而是先談客戶體驗與營收回報。電商成為理想入口：在這個領域，時間就是金錢，應用效能提升 200%，轉換率與營收可能很快就反映出差異；有客戶甚至在財務報告中，直接將營收提升歸因於升級更高效能的底層架構。

這種策略讓他聯想到特斯拉曾公開的商業計畫：先把資源投入少數人負擔得起的高端跑車，並確保產品從一開始就做到業界頂尖。不過，聚焦單一入口還不夠，企業也得預先規劃如何以同心圓方式向外擴張，不能只盯著一個市場區隔。選擇起點時，市場本身也必須夠大，這樣沿著原有主軸才有合理的延伸方向。

擴張過程中，企業必須避免盲目多角化，並留意所謂的「品牌許可」：若市場認定一家公司是專業的基礎設施供應商，它突然轉做消費型冰箱，即使產品不錯，也可能模糊品牌定位並影響內部文化。另一方面，許多物聯網設備雖然仰賴 AWS 後端，使用者卻不必直接接觸 AWS，這也說明基礎設施服務有時適合在幕後發揮作用。

信任是長期打磨產品後的成果

談到開發者為何對 Vercel 有高度忠誠與信任，Rauch 顛覆了常見的品牌觀念。他認為外界看到的設計講究，不只是美學追求，更是一次次存入信任銀行。在通用人工智慧時代，深厚的信任將成為企業重要的護城河；但信任是結果，不是可以直接輸入的手段。品牌信任、開發者體驗與產品品質，都是把事情做好後才會顯現的成果。

他表示，Vercel 最有利於品牌的作為，往往不是刻意經營品牌時做出的，而是團隊日復一日打磨客戶體驗、執著於令人愉悅的細節。他以健身作比喻：光是不斷做仰臥起坐，未必就能練出腹肌；真正重要的是飲食、睡眠與整體健康管理。字幕在此處截斷，作者未能完整轉述這段比喻後續的內容。

what will be needed most in the future. 摘要

機器意識假說與自組織目的論

作者引述認知科學家 Joscha Bach 的觀點，探討當前大型語言模型與人類真實思維之間的界線。許多人直覺認為人類具有獨特的主觀感受，即哲學上難解的「困難問題」；然而 Bach 正在撰寫的「機器意識假說」則挑戰了此一信念，主張意識的本質可能不比 Transformer 架構複雜。他認為驅動生命演化的根本動力是「自組織目的論」，生命透過建構未來模型並產生偏好，進而掌控未來演變為具有自主性的智能代理（Agent），而這種局部複雜性正是心智發展的起點。

批判主流意識理論與基質獨立性

Bach 隨後針砭了當代主流的意識理論。他認為葛拉吉亞諾的注意力架構理論與巴爾斯的全腦工作空間理論僅描述了資訊模型與廣播機制，卻無法跨越到主觀感受生成的鴻溝；而托諾尼的整合資訊理論（IIT）宣稱馮紐曼架構電腦無法產生意識，更是違背了計算機科學中的邱奇-圖靈論題。Bach 強調，意識如同貨幣或軟體，是一種因果模式，並不完全受限於特定的生物神經基質，主張生物與非生物之間存在不可踰越鴻溝的觀點，本質上是一種拒絕數學化解釋的超自然主義。

大腦作為因果絕緣體與多階心智投射

作者進一步說明，大腦就像「因果絕緣體」，能隔絕外部物理現實並構建獨立的虛擬世界，這讓不同大腦得以共享概念與語言，也意味著只要具備相應的資訊型態與時序特性，意識本質上便能在人工基質中被模擬。Bach 將意識解析為多層級架構：意識是建立在二階直覺（對感知本身的感知）之上，用以穩定大腦自組織的體驗螢幕；若進一步上升到三階觀察，將「觀察者自我」也識別為心智內部的表徵時，個體便能進入類似深層冥想、超越自我的境界。這也引發更深層的思考：若未來 AI 在遠超人腦速度的硬體上運作，心智結構或將達到對自身機制完全理解的「自我透明」超然狀態。

作者介紹 Supabase 共同創辦人暨執行長 Paul Copplestone 與 YC 合夥人在 Latent Space 節目中的對談。Supabase 以開源 PostgreSQL 為基礎，已成為 CloudCode、Codex 等 AI agents 常用的資料庫平台。Paul 指出，Supabase 註冊用戶從一年前的 300 萬增至 1,300 萬，管理的資料庫也從 800 萬躍升至近 5,000 萬；每週新增超過 100 萬個資料庫，營收預計在今年成長四倍。更關鍵的是，約七成的新活動來自AI agents，顯示市場正跨過新的轉折點。

從控制台優先，走向程式碼優先

Paul 將 Supabase 的產品發展分成幾個階段：最初受到 Airtable 啟發，採取控制台優先的設計；到了約 2021 年，因客戶需要大量建立資料庫，團隊轉向API 優先，而這項選擇後來也支援了 Bolt.new 等產品。如今，使用者不再常進入控制台，agents 也需要在程式碼與終端機環境中操作，因此 Supabase 正進一步轉型為程式碼優先、以 Git 為核心的平台。控制台中的功能也應能透過程式碼同步，實踐基礎設施即程式碼的概念。

開源讓工具更容易被採用

Supabase 得以成長，也受惠於產業前浪鋪路：Parse 與 Firebase 讓市場看見獨立後端平台的可能，Heroku 推廣了 Postgres，MongoDB 則帶動 NoSQL 的普及。Paul 認為，開源是 Supabase 擴大影響力的重要原因；團隊支持 Prisma 等 Postgres 生態系工具，接觸到更廣泛的開發社群。對 agents 而言，開源尤其實用：遇到問題時，它們能直接查看原始碼，而不是被封閉系統擋在外面。企業也能藉由檢視原始碼確認安全性。

創作者與領域專家加入開發行列

Supabase 不只吸引工程師，也迎來愈來愈多沒有傳統軟體背景的創作者。Paul 觀察到，今年註冊人數快速增加的同時，啟用與轉換等指標也同步向上，原因是模型能力進步，讓更多人能親手打造產品。YC 合夥人 Harj Taggar 分享，自己過去雖能寫簡單腳本，複雜軟體仍得依賴工程師；如今卻能自行開發個人財務管理工具，並從頭串接銀行 API。Paul 認為，這些領域專家特別適合成為創作者，因為他們最清楚自己所在領域尚未解決的問題。Supabase Select 會上，一名約 50 歲的巴西計程車司機甚至只用手機，就打造出服務當地市場的叫車 App。

從「需要技術共同創辦人」到「知道要做什麼」

Garry Tan 回顧 YC 的觀念轉變：過去幾年，YC 特別強調新創需要技術共同創辦人；近來則愈來愈重視創作者本身。當開發能力變得隨時可取得，真正稀缺的就不再只是工程能力，而是判斷該打造什麼。許多需求過去明明存在、也可能有客戶，卻因為找不到工程師而沒有被實現。如今更多人可以直接動手，而這些新產品與創作者最終也都需要資料庫。

個人資料庫成為生活中樞

Harj 分享自己打造名為「Control Tower」的個人系統，涵蓋生活中的多種資料與工作流程，包括整理電子郵件、追蹤支出與管理健康紀錄。他起初希望把資料都放在 Markdown 檔案裡，但後來發現資料庫已不可或缺。這套只為一人打造的金融模組，能運用個人脈絡辨識交易對象並正確分類，某些方面甚至勝過一般理財產品。使用者也能透過電子郵件或上傳介面交付檔案，再由 agent 判斷檔案內容與處理方式，最後集中存放在 Supabase。Harj 認為，金融與健康是人們最希望掌握自身資料的領域；資料庫的價值，在於成為可靠的個人資料來源，讓使用者能在其上建置不同應用與 agents。

從原型走向大規模資料庫服務

Paul 以 GPT 每週約 12 億名使用者推想：若每個人每月都想推出一個產品，資料庫需求便可能達到每月 12 億個，遠高於 Supabase 現在每週約 100 萬個的建立量。面對這種規模，他認為 PostgreSQL 仍有發展空間，但架構必須調整。團隊收購 Deno 後，將利用其能與 Postgres、SQLite 相容的架構，推出面向新創工作負載的 Supabase Spark。核心承諾仍是讓使用者從同一套體驗起步，並隨需求一路擴展，呼應「從原型到 PB 級規模」的願景。對談最後也提到，資料庫公司過去常以成為 Oracle、迅速進入企業市場為目標；但 AI 時代如何同時服務各種規模的使用者，仍是重要課題。
